tickets.title: P2-27: /api/riskguard/config POST validates no VALUES, and the editable UI is about to make that reachable by hand
tickets.defect:
`addons/McpBridgeAddOn.cs`, `private object RiskGuardConfig(string body)` (around line 6539).

The write path is hardened against the wrong SHAPE and not against wrong CONTENT. `P1-80` stopped it persisting a file nothing ever read back. `P2-41` made it MERGE the partial body onto the live config instead of deserializing the body alone, which had been giving every omitted field its DEFAULT and silently resetting Mode, MinShadowSessions and every StopGuard value while replying "applied".

What neither addressed: nothing looks at what the values MEAN. The merged RiskConfig goes straight to `SaveAndReloadConfig`, and `SaveAndReloadConfig` DOES NOT RUN PREFLIGHT. So a config that cannot pass preflight is written to RiskGuard/config.json and reloaded happily, and the guard comes up DISARMED at the next restart -- with nothing about the file looking wrong.

That is survivable while the only writer is a deliberate API call. It stops being survivable the moment the editable UI lands, because the entire point of that page is an operator changing limits quickly, and the failure is silent and delayed: the write says `applied`, the page re-renders the value it just sent, and the guard is not protecting anything after the next restart.
tickets.spec:
TWO changes.

1. NEW FILE `addons/BridgeGuardConfigEdit.cs`, namespace `NinjaTrader.NinjaScript.AddOns`, holding ALL the logic:

```csharp
public static class BridgeGuardConfigEdit
{
    public static string Refuse(string mode, double trailingDrawdown, int minShadowSessions)
}
```

Returns `null` when the config is acceptable, otherwise a single operator-readable sentence naming the FIELD that is wrong and what would have been accepted.

It must name NO NinjaTrader type -- no Account, no Instrument, no RiskConfig. Primitives only. That is the whole reason it can be executed by the harness.

Rules, and the tests pin each one:
  * `mode` must be one of shadow / live / disabled, compared case-insensitively. Anything else is refused, and the refusal must NAME the valid ones.
  * `trailingDrawdown` must be strictly positive. Zero is refused: it is not a tight limit, it is no protection, and it reads as configured in every surface that lists it.
  * `trailingDrawdown` negative is refused.
  * `minShadowSessions` negative is refused.
  * Anything else is ACCEPTED -- return null.

A null or whitespace `mode` should be treated as "not being changed" and accepted, NOT refused: the endpoint takes PARTIAL bodies by design (that is P2-41's merge) and refusing an omitted field would make every partial write fail.

2. `addons/McpBridgeAddOn.cs`, inside `RiskGuardConfig`: after the merge produces `cfg` and BEFORE `SaveAndReloadConfig`, call `BridgeGuardConfigEdit.Refuse(...)` with the values from the MERGED config, and if the answer is non-empty RETURN an error object naming it. Do not apply. Do not log and continue.

Read the merged values off `cfg`; if a property name is not obvious from the surrounding code, prefer reading it from `mergedJson` rather than inventing a property that does not exist.
tickets.context:
WHY REFUSAL-SHAPED AND NOT CLAMPING. A clamp turns an operator's 0 into a 2500 they did not choose and did not see -- the limit they are then held to is not the one on their screen. Refusing is the only answer that leaves the operator's model of their own protection correct. This repo's whole `configured / evaluated / enforcing` family is four shipped defects that are all one thing: a surface stating protection that does not exist.

WHY THE REFUSAL MUST NAME THE FIELD. `P1-90`'s resolver refuses an unresolvable account by listing the 96 real ones, and that is the standard here. A UI renders this string next to an input; "invalid configuration" is not actionable in a form with a dozen of them.

WHY AN UNKNOWN MODE IS THE FIRST RULE. `P1-72` has REGRESSED TWICE on this codebase and it is always the same shape: a surface advertises or accepts a value that nothing implements. `enabled` is the obvious thing an operator types for `live`.

WHY THE ORDER MATTERS. Validating after `SaveAndReloadConfig` is a report, not a gate -- the live engine has already been reloaded by the time you would speak.

WHY A SOURCE ASSERTION ON THE CONDITION AND NOT THE CALL. Four mutants in this project have beaten a source gate meant to prove a value is USED, each weaker than the last assumed: called, then mentioned, then returned-nearby, then the condition neutered to `if (false)` leaving an unreachable `return` sitting in the text. The test therefore requires `Refuse(...)` to be followed by a real `string.IsNullOrEmpty` condition.

tickets.note_expect_green:
Only assertions that ACTUALLY FAIL at baseline belong here -- expect_green is matched against the runner FAILURE LINES and means red-now-green-after. Two sub-assertions were listed here and the loop REFUSED the ticket for it, correctly: they sit behind an if (!Refused(reason)) return; guard, so while the class does not exist they do not FAIL, they never RUN. They are still enforced -- the loop requires the whole suite green at the end -- they just cannot be part of the test-first gate.

These are the assertions actually RED at the 396/9 baseline. The load-bearing one is 'A valid config ... is ACCEPTED': a validator that refuses everything satisfies all six negative assertions, and this repo has shipped exactly that -- P3-30's audit fired on correctly protected accounts behind three positive-only acceptance tests. For a refuser, the acceptance case is the one that proves it works.

Two of these assertions passed VACUOUSLY on their first run: CallRefuse answers a `___CLASS_MISSING___` sentinel while the class does not exist, which is non-empty, so a bare IsNullOrEmpty check was satisfied by the class being ABSENT. They now route through Refused(), which rejects the sentinel. Do not reintroduce a sentinel-shaped return value from Refuse().
